title: Experimental voice input with explicit recognition providers
summary: Voice input is an optional, default-off bundle with an explicit recognition provider chosen by id and no fallback between providers. Recordings and transcripts stay transient: recognition only inserts text into the draft and never starts a turn or writes a session event.
firstReason: The rules are about user control and privacy, not about JavaScript: no silent provider fallback (a local failure must not upload speech to a cloud service), no resources allocated until used, and late results discarded when the draft or session changed. The recording widget is a browser island under DH-ADR-3; the provider registry is a Go component.

title: Native CUA objects independent of evaluator ownership
summary: The shared computer-use (CUA) library owns application and window objects, consent and logged dispatch; the macOS package owns the Swift helper and its connection. The object API has no interpreter of its own: it takes a dispatcher, so every operation goes through the normal tool path for authorization, logging and image admission.
firstReason: Keeping the object API free of an evaluator means variable persistence and cancellation are decided once, by the execution host. The Swift helper is already a separate native process, so a Go host talks to it the same way.

title: Application consent for native Computer Use
summary: The computer-use executor asks the user for consent per target application before any operation on it, using the user-questions service, and stores grants per profile. This consent is separate from general tool approval and from operating-system privileges.
firstReason: macOS privileges authorize the helper, not the user's choice of application, and retained window objects can outlive a decision. Enforcement at every dispatch is a security rule that must hold in Go.

title: Shared native CUA process with Agent-scoped state
summary: One native computer-use helper process per user and per executable content digest is shared by all agents and hosts, elected by file locks and ended when its last connection closes. It runs as a signed application started through the system launcher so that it holds its own privacy permissions.
firstReason: The constraint is in macOS: screen-capture identity follows the executable path, and permissions follow the launched application. It applies to a Go host exactly as it does to Node.

title: Continuous CUA hover without cross-call ownership
summary: Computer-use hover is an explicit mouse-move operation that never presses a button and never restores the previous pointer position afterwards. No operation gives an agent ownership of an application across calls.
firstReason: Restoring the pointer, or priming with a click, dismissed the hover content. The rule of no ownership across calls keeps the shared helper simple. The behaviour belongs to the native helper and is unaffected by the host language.

title: Background hover and screenshot coordinates
summary: By default hover uses an accessibility route that does not move the user's real pointer; moving the system pointer needs an explicit request and, when configured, user approval. The host converts screenshot pixel coordinates to window points so that the model does not have to.
firstReason: Not disturbing the user's pointer, and not making the model do display-scaling arithmetic, are product rules implemented in the helper and the provider's geometry code.

title: Durable Computer Use consent within one profile
summary: Computer-use grants and per-conversation decisions are kept in the profile's domain storage, not in plugin configuration or process memory. Every operation reopens the state under the profile file lock, and revocation generations stop a stale handle or a late answer from restoring access.
firstReason: Grants in configuration tied each change to config reconciliation, and in-memory decisions were lost on restart and invisible to other host processes. Revocation that holds across processes is a security requirement.

title: macOS consent shared by bundle identifier
summary: Computer-use consent on macOS is keyed by the application's bundle identifier, so one decision covers all installed versions. The executable path is the fallback identity when there is no bundle identifier.
firstReason: Path and signature identities split one application into many grants and excluded unsigned development builds. The identity rule lives with the native helper.

title: Development signing identity for source-built CUA helpers
summary: Source builds of the computer-use helper are a separate 'Dev' application with its own bundle identifier, optionally signed with a developer-chosen certificate, so that macOS permissions survive rebuilds and do not replace the release helper's grants.
firstReason: macOS ties privacy grants to the bundle identifier and the code signature. Anyone who builds the Swift helper from source for the Go harness meets the same constraint, so the development variant is kept; the signing set-up guide in the note is contributor workflow.

title: CUA scoped surfaces and separated input capabilities
summary: Computer Use (CUA, the capability that drives desktop applications) exposes one shared surface for operations common to applications and windows, with application-only and window-only operations added on top. Static provider capabilities are fixed at install and kept apart from runtime permissions, and keyboard input separates a key from its modifiers (`pressKey`) and from single key-down or key-up events (`sendKeyEvent`).
firstReason: The split is an interface design that Go expresses directly with embedded interfaces, and it keeps window behaviour from depending on an application-level capability check.

title: Serve Computer Use to other harnesses as an MCP server
summary: Computer Use is offered to other agent harnesses as an MCP stdio server that runs inside a standalone `cua-mcp` profile. One stdio connection owns one Agent, created before the transport opens and disposed at end of input, and each call runs through the ordinary tool pipeline with no model step.
firstReason: Serving a capability over MCP through the same tool pipeline keeps consent, cancellation and state ownership in one place. In Go the profile is a configuration of compiled-in components (DH-ADR-4), so the optional-bundle packaging part of the note does not carry over.

title: AX traversal defaults and per-read limits
summary: An accessibility-tree read takes `maxElements` and `maxDepth` from the request when given and from provider configuration otherwise, so a caller can go deeper for one read without raising the defaults for every later read. The native provider still enforces its own ceilings.
firstReason: A per-call override under a provider-enforced ceiling is a language-neutral way to bound work and output.

title: CUA programs outside the PTC preset
summary: Agents on the PTC preset get the raw `cua` tool; every other agent gets `cua_run_code`, a program tool built from the shared program-tool factory with one isolated, state-retaining runtime per agent. Registration is by agent scope, so enabling or disabling the provider affects existing and later agents without editing presets.
firstReason: One tool form per agent and scope-owned registration follow the cordis ownership model the Go port already has. It depends on the Go design keeping a program runtime (see the PTC notes); that runtime is a separate process upstream as well.

title: CUA program tool for Agents without a preset
summary: Agents that join no preset (SDK, headless and ACP applications) also receive `cua_run_code`; only agents on the configured preset receive raw `cua`. The preset registry becomes an optional dependency, and the provider recomputes each live agent's tool form when the registry loads or unloads.
firstReason: Without it the default Computer Use configuration has no effect in headless and SDK hosts. Optional dependencies that re-evaluate on load and unload are a cordis feature the Go port has.
